items.title: [Codex] [2/2] Add thread catalog metadata subscriptions
items.body:
## Why

`thread/list` is a paginated snapshot. A client that has loaded only part of the catalog cannot learn when an unseen thread is created or its sidebar metadata changes. Using `thread/resume` for this would load every runtime and subscribe the client to detailed turn and item traffic merely to keep a thread list current.

This is the second PR in a two-PR stack. #29894 provides the store-owned invalidation stream; this PR exposes it as a metadata-only app-server subscription.

## What changed

Adds the connection-scoped, opt-in `threadCatalog/subscribe` request and future-only `threadCatalog/changed` notification. Changes are global rather than filter-specific:

- `upsert` carries a complete `ThreadSummary` suitable for rendering and ordering a catalog row.
- `delete` carries the removed thread ID.
- `invalidate` tells the client that it must rebuild its snapshot.

`ThreadSummary` contains persisted catalog metadata, including `parentThreadId`, `source`, nickname, and role. It deliberately excludes turns, items, messages, tool state, loaded runtime state, and runtime status. Catalog delivery also shares the existing thread-list state boundary so a delete is not observed before app-server cleanup completes.

## Client contract

1. Call `threadCatalog/subscribe` and buffer notifications.
2. Build the authoritative snapshot with `thread/list`; for subagents, page with `ancestorThreadId`.
3. Apply buffered and future upserts and deletes idempotently by thread ID. Repeat the snapshot after `invalidate`.
4. Merge the existing global `thread/status/changed` feed by thread ID for active or idle runtime state.

The feed has no replay. Reconnects repeat the subscribe-and-list sequence, and mutations missed while disconnected are recovered only by that fresh snapshot. Old clients receive no new events because the subscription is opt-in; Codex Apps must version-gate the request and retain its existing startup behavior on older app servers.

## Scope

This API enables history-independent thread and subagent discovery. It does not expose spawn-edge `open | closed` state, replace completion notifications, provide inherited transcripts, or reconcile global startup state by itself.

## Verification

All 253 app-server protocol tests pass. Public JSON-RPC coverage verifies metadata changes for a thread the client never listed, deletion, omission of runtime/detail fields, and normal subagent creation metadata. Schema generation, TUI test compilation, scoped Clippy, and formatting also pass.

items.body:
### What variant of Codex are you using?

CLI

### What version of Codex are you using?

`codex-cli 0.141.0`

### What happened?

A `Stop` hook's `systemMessage` is always rendered in the TUI with the `warning:` prefix, even when the message is purely informational. There is no info/notice severity available to an end-of-turn hook, so passive status lines (cost/usage summaries, routing info, "all checks passed", etc.) are surfaced as warnings.

Example — this Stop hook output:

```json
{ "systemMessage": "Auto-routing savings this session: ~$0.94 (vs <reference-model>)" }
```

renders as:

```
• Stop hook (completed)
  warning: Auto-routing savings this session: ~$0.94 (vs <reference-model>)
```

### Why this isn't fixable from the hook side

In `codex-rs/hooks/src/events/stop.rs`, `parse_completed` maps `systemMessage` unconditionally to `HookOutputEntryKind::Warning`:

```rust
if let Some(system_message) = parsed.universal.system_message {
    entries.push(HookOutputEntry {
        kind: HookOutputEntryKind::Warning,   // forced
        text: system_message,
    });
}
```

For a `Stop` hook the only reachable entry kinds are `Warning` (from `systemMessage`), `Stop` (from `continue:false` + `stopReason`), `Feedback` (from `decision:"block"`), and `Error`. The neutral `HookOutputEntryKind::HookContext` (`hook context:` prefix, added in #17266) is **never produced** for `Stop`, and `hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext` isn't an accepted `Stop` field (`deny_unknown_fields`).

The available alternatives don't work as passive notes:
- `decision:"block"` + `reason` → renders as `feedback:` **but force-continues the turn** (injects a new user prompt).
- exit code `2` + stderr → also treated as a turn continuation.
- plain-text stdout → invalid for `Stop`.

So `systemMessage` → `warning:` is the only passive, user-visible channel for an end-of-turn hook, and it's hardwired to the warning label.

### What I expected

A way for an end-of-turn (and ideally any) hook to surface a **non-warning informational note**. Options that would solve it:

1. Add an info/notice entry kind (e.g. rendered as `note:` / `info:`) selectable from hook output — for example an optional severity on `systemMessage`, or a dedicated field.
2. Allow `Stop` hooks to emit a neutral `hook context:`-style entry that is shown to the user (not injected into the model turn).

### Why it matters

Stop hooks are a natural place for end-of-turn informational summaries (usage/cost, routing decisions, lint/test status). Today every one of these reads as a warning, which trains users to ignore the prefix and makes legitimately useful notes feel alarming.

### Related (but distinct)

- #25403 (quiet mode) and #15497 / #19383 — about *suppressing* hook output, not relabeling an info note.
- #21753 (Claude hook parity) and #19385 (`additionalContext` in `PreToolUse`) — adjacent, but neither requests an info-severity user-visible entry for `Stop`.

items.title: fix: fall back to gpt-5.4 for unsupported Bedrock models
items.body:
## Why

#27129 made the memory extraction and consolidation helpers use provider-specific model defaults, but task title generation can still start an Amazon Bedrock thread with the OpenAI model slug `gpt-5.4-mini`. Bedrock's authoritative catalog only exposes its prefixed model IDs, so Mantle rejects that request with a 404 and the failure can surface as a misleading `Turn error` on the main thread.

Handling this at the static model catalog boundary keeps the compatibility rule in codex-rs for every client, while avoiding a Bedrock-specific special case in session or app-server code.

## What changed

- Added an optional `unsupported_model_fallback` to `StaticModelsManager` construction.
- Updated `StaticModelsManager::get_default_model` to use that fallback only when a client explicitly requests a model absent from the authoritative catalog.

items.title: [codex] Flush trailing realtime transcript on session end
items.body:
## Why

Codex core already owns the realtime transcript buffer, but session teardown discarded transcript entries received after the last handoff. An app-side continuity cache cannot make that tail durable in the Codex thread, and teardown can also race a handoff event that has been parsed but not yet routed.

Core should persist the final transcript delta before it reports the realtime session closed, regardless of whether the boundary is an explicit close, transport/error shutdown, session replacement, or full session cleanup.

## What changed

- Split the realtime transcript cursor into requested and committed handoff positions, so a parsed-but-unrouted handoff remains eligible for finalization.
- Serialize handoff routing/commit with teardown and take the uncommitted transcript tail at most once.
- Route every core-owned realtime stop boundary through one finalizer that records a hidden `developer` `<realtime_delegation>` fragment and flushes the rollout before emitting `thread/realtime/closed`.
- Bound the persisted fragment to 8,000 tokens and XML-escape transcript content.
- Add focused API and core coverage for empty tails, one-time persistence, handoff dedupe, repeated close, and transport close.

## Validation

- `just test -p codex-api` (134 passed)
- `just test -p codex-core realtime_transcript_tail` (4 passed)
- `just test -p codex-core inbound_handoff_request_starts_turn` (2 passed)
- `just fix -p codex-api`
- `just fix -p codex-core`
- `just fmt`

I also attempted the complete `just test -p codex-core` suite. It reached 2,778 passing tests; the remaining 77 failures were caused by local sandbox/proxy write restrictions, missing separately built test binaries, and one unrelated code-mode timing assertion.

## Limitations

This provides a durability barrier for normal async teardown paths. A process crash, `SIGKILL`, or power loss before the finalizer runs would require a separate incremental journal/WAL design.

items.title: Permission / approval mode selection does not persist for new or existing threads

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: sandbox
labels.description: Issues related to permissions or sandboxing

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

labels.name: session
labels.description: Issues involving session (thread) management, resuming, forking, naming, archiving

items.body:
## Summary

Permission / approval mode selection is not reliably persisted for either new threads or already-loaded existing threads.

This originally looked like only a loaded-thread `thread/resume` problem, but there is a broader desktop-visible failure:

- On an existing loaded thread, changing approval / permission mode through resume appears to work in the UI, but the live thread keeps the old effective settings.
- On a new thread, the permission picker allows selecting non-workspace options such as **Full access**, but after the thread starts / first prompt executes, the effective state falls back to **workspace**.
- The dropdown state can therefore look selectable before submission while the running thread state does not reflect the selected mode.

## New-thread repro

1. Open Codex desktop.
2. Start a new thread.
3. In the permission / approval picker, choose a non-workspace mode, for example **Full access**.
4. Send the first prompt / start the thread.
5. Reopen or inspect the permission picker.

Observed: the running thread shows **workspace** selected again instead of the selected mode.

Expected: the selected permission profile should be sent to app-server, reflected in the `thread/start` response, and used as the thread's effective permission state. If policy or requirements disallow the requested mode, the UI should show that explicitly rather than appearing to accept it and silently reverting.

## Existing loaded-thread repro

1. Start a thread with default / read-only-ish settings.
2. Materialize the rollout with a simple turn.
3. Resume or switch back to the already-loaded thread while requesting different approval / permission settings, for example `approvalPolicy` plus `permissions = ":danger-full-access"`.
4. Inspect the resume response or subsequent effective settings.

Observed: loaded-thread `thread/resume` previously ignored supported overrides and kept the old effective permission mode.

Expected: supported resume overrides should be validated and applied to the live thread, and the response should reflect the effective settings.

## Suggested fix candidates

Two linked commits on a fork cover the two parts found so far:

1. Loaded-thread backend fix:
   https://github.com/andrewsohrabi/codex/commit/94e81ea40cc0fbb88f01aaa035b32157e5b34419

   This adds a regression test for loaded `thread/resume` applying `approvalPolicy` + `permissions`, then routes supported loaded-resume overrides through the same validated thread-settings path used by `thread/settings/update`. Startup-only fields such as `config`, `baseInstructions`, and `developerInstructions` remain ignored while the thread is already loaded.

2. New-thread schema / client-contract fix:
   https://github.com/andrewsohrabi/codex/commit/d39d601907a5328bb74be44c296c29c579b56558

   This adds coverage proving stable generated TypeScript includes permission-profile selection for thread lifecycle requests, then exposes `permissions` plus `activePermissionProfile` for `thread/start`, `thread/resume`, and `thread/fork` in the stable protocol fixtures. Without this, generated stable clients can list/read permission profiles but cannot cleanly send the selected named profile or read profile provenance from lifecycle responses.

Compare:
https://github.com/openai/codex/compare/main...andrewsohrabi:codex/permissions-fix

## Validation run locally

Focused checks passed:

- `just test -p codex-app-server-protocol generated_ts_optional_nullable_fields_only_in_params`
- `just test -p codex-app-server-protocol`
- `just test -p codex-app-server thread_start_applies_named_permission_profile thread_resume_loaded_thread_applies_permission_overrides`

Full `just test -p codex-app-server` was attempted. In this managed sandbox it ended with unrelated local environment failures: nested macOS `sandbox-exec` returns exit 71 (`sandbox_apply: Operation not permitted`), one executor MCP test cannot locate `target/debug/codex`, and a few file-watch / sandboxed image or file-change tests time out. The permission regressions above passed inside that run.

`just fix -p ...` and `just fmt` were also attempted but are blocked by the local toolchain / sandbox (`cargo clippy` and `cargo fmt` missing, `dotslash` missing, and `uv` cannot initialize its cache). `git diff --check` passes.

items.title: exec-server: handle post-init requests concurrently
items.body:
## Intent

Allow independent exec-server RPCs to make progress while another request is long-polling, without weakening the `initialize` / `initialized` ordering contract.

## Implementation

- Keep `initialize` requests and notifications inline as handshake ordering barriers; spawn other request handlers after latching initialization state at admission, bounded to the transport channel capacity per connection.
- Wake the connection loop on request completion or transport disconnect and cancel outstanding requests before session detach.
- Clear incomplete process-start reservations left by cancelled handlers.
- Document that concurrent responses may arrive out of order.

## Validation

- `just test -p codex-exec-server` (289 passed, 2 skipped)
- Added coverage for pipelined responses, initialization-order violations, duplicate-initialize wire ordering, long-read concurrency, bounded request admission, idle task failure, response sink failure, process-start cleanup, and disconnect/resume.

items.title: [codex] Flush trailing realtime transcript tail
items.body:
## Why

A realtime session can end after more transcript has accumulated than was included in its last handoff. That tail already lives in core's active transcript state, but the stop path aborted the realtime input/fanout tasks before routing it, so the final bit of the conversation could disappear before `thread/realtime/closed`.

This behavior is still being evaluated, so clients must opt in per realtime session. Omitted or false leaves shutdown behavior unchanged.

## What changed

- Add optional `flushTranscriptTailOnSessionEnd` to `thread/realtime/start`, defaulting to false in app-server.
- Expose an idempotent `take_transcript_tail()` from the existing active transcript state using `last_handoff_entry_count`.
- When enabled, let shutdown cancel the input owner cleanly and publish at most one final existing `<realtime_delegation>` with the remaining text in `<transcript_delta>`.
- Have the existing fanout drain already-parsed events before routing that final delegation, so a queued handoff wins first and is not duplicated in the tail.
- Flush realtime shutdown before ordinary session task abort during core cleanup.

## Validation

- `just test -p codex-app-server-protocol`
- `just test -p codex-app-server realtime_conversation_stop_emits_closed_notification`
- `just test -p codex-core conversation_transport_close_`
- `just test -p codex-core conversation_close_routes_only_remaining_transcript_tail_once`
- scoped `just fix` for `codex-app-server-protocol`, `codex-app-server`, `codex-protocol`, and `codex-core`
- `just fmt`
